p.seg: Dào Yuán
Lǎozǐ said:
"There is a thing formed out of chaos,
born before Heaven and Earth.
It is only an image, without form;
deep and obscure,
silent and still,
its sound cannot be heard.
I forcibly give it a name,
and call it 'Dao'."
Now, Dao,
is so high it cannot be reached,
so deep it cannot be fathomed.
It encompasses Heaven and Earth,
and receives its existence from the formless.
Its source flows unceasingly,
emptying itself without becoming full.
Turbid, but made clear slowly by stillness.
It gives without end,
without beginning or end.
Rolled up, it does not fill a handful;
contracted, it can expand.
Hidden, it can be bright;
soft, it can be hard.
It contains Yin and emits Yang,
thus manifesting the three luminaries.
Mountains are high because of it,
The depths are used for deep pools,
animals use them to run,
birds use them to fly,
scaled creatures use them to swim,
phoenixes use them to soar,
and the stars and calendar use them to move;
use loss to gain existence,
use humility to gain honor,
use retreat to gain precedence.
In ancient times, the Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng),
grasped the essence of the Dao,
and established themselves in the center,
their spirits wandered with transformation,
thereby pacifying the four directions.
Therefore, they were able to
move Heaven and steady Earth,
rotate ceaselessly without fail,
the waters flow without stopping,
and begin and end with all things.
The wind rises and clouds gather,
thunder sounds and rain falls,
all responding without end,
having been carved and polished,
return again to simplicity.
Acting through non-action
and conforming to life and death,
speaking through non-speaking
and comprehending morality and virtue,
Tián yú wú jīn
result in harmony;
having myriad differences
yet all find convenience in life.
Harmonizing *yīnyáng*,
regulating the four seasons,
adjusting the five elements,
moistening grasses and trees,
permeating metals and stones,
birds and beasts are large,
fine hairs are lustrous,
bird eggs do not spoil,
animal fetuses are not stillborn,
fathers have no sorrow of losing sons,
elder brothers have no grief of mourning younger brothers,
children are not orphaned,
women are not widowed,
rainbows are not seen,
thieves do not roam,
all are brought about by embracing virtue.
The Way of the Great Constant
gives birth to things but does not possess them,
achieves transformation but does not control them,
the myriad things
rely on it to live,
but do not know its virtue,
rely on it to die,
but cannot resent it.
Accumulating and hoarding
does not increase wealth;
giving and receiving
does not increase poverty.
Dim and indistinct,
it cannot be represented in form;
indistinct and dim,
its use is inexhaustible.
Deep and dark,
it responds to transformations without shape;
continuous and pervasive,
it does not move in vain;
it accords with the coiling and stretching of hardness and softness;
it accords with the rising and falling of *yīn* and *yáng*.
Lǎozǐ said:
A great person is serene and without thought,
calm and without worry.
He takes the sky as his canopy,
the earth as his carriage,
the four seasons as his horses,
and *yīn* and *yáng* as his driver.
He travels where there are no roads,
wanders without weariness,
and emerges from no gate.
To take the sky as a canopy means there is nothing not covered;
to take the earth as a carriage means there is nothing not carried;
to take the four seasons as horses means there is nowhere not driven;
To employ *yīnyáng*
means nothing is left unprepared.
Therefore, one is swift yet unagitated,
far-reaching yet untired,
the four limbs are not taxed,
intelligence is not diminished,
and one illuminates and perceives all under Heaven.
This is grasping the essence of the Dao,
and observing the boundless realm.
Therefore, affairs under Heaven cannot be forced.
Follow their natural course and propel them forward.
The transformations of the myriad things cannot be fully fathomed.
Grasp their essential tendencies and return to them.
Therefore, the sage cultivates the root within,
and does not outwardly embellish the branches.
He hones his spirit,
suppresses his intellect and contrivances,
and in tranquil non-action, there is nothing he does not accomplish;
in non-governance, there is nothing ungoverned.
What is meant by "non-action"
is not acting before things do;
what is meant by "non-governance"
is not altering the natural order;
what is meant by "nothing ungoverned"
is acting in accordance with the mutual naturalness of things.
Lǎozǐ said:
One who governs the people by holding to the Dao
Events arise and are followed;
things move and are conformed to;
the transformations of all things invariably respond,
the changes of a hundred years invariably correspond.
Therefore, the Dao is
emptiness,
simplicity,
purity and tranquility,
gentleness and weakness,
and pure simplicity.
These five qualities
are the image of the Dao.
Emptiness is the dwelling place of the Dao,
simplicity is the essence of the Dao,
purity and tranquility are the mirror of the Dao,
gentleness and weakness are the function of the Dao.
Reversal is the constant of the Dao,
gentleness is the firmness of the Dao,
weakness is the strength of the Dao.
Pure simplicity is the substance of the Dao.
Emptiness means that the mind contains nothing.
Simplicity means that the mind has no worries.
When desires and cravings are not held,
emptiness reaches its peak.
When there is nothing that is liked or disliked,
simplicity reaches its peak.
To be unified and unchanging,
tranquility reaches its peak.
Not mixed with external things is the utmost purity.
Having neither worry nor joy is the utmost virtue.
The way the most perfect man governs
is to abandon his intelligence,
extinguish his embellishments,
rely on the Dao and abolish wisdom,
and together with the people, proceed from impartiality.
Restrict what he guards,
reduce what he seeks,
eliminate what entices and admires,
remove his desires and lusts,
diminish his thoughts and worries.
Restricting what he guards leads to clarity;
reducing what he seeks leads to attainment.
Therefore, using the internal to control the external,
a hundred affairs are not neglected.
If the internal can be attained, then the external can be governed.
The attainment of the internal
brings peace to the five viscera,
calms thoughts and worries,
strengthens sinews and bones,
and sharpens ears and eyes.
The Great Dao is broad and even;
departing from oneself is not far.
Seeking it afar
leads to going and returning.
Lǎozǐ said:
The sage forgets about governing others,
and instead focuses on governing himself.
He values forgetting about power and position,
and instead focuses on self-attainment.
Self-attainment means the world attains me;
he finds joy in forgetting about wealth and status,
and instead focuses on harmony.
Understanding that one's self is greater while the world is smaller,
he is close to the Dao.
Therefore it is said:
"Attain utmost emptiness,
hold firmly to stillness.
The myriad things arise together,
and I thereby observe their return."
The Dao,
molds and smelts the myriad things,
having no form from beginning to end,
silent and unmoving,
greatly pervading the chaotic darkness,
deep, vast, and great, cannot be considered external;
analyzing a hair or splitting a grain of awn cannot be considered internal.
Without walls of a house,
it gives rise to the totality of existence and non-existence.
The true person embodies it with emptiness,
equanimity,
purity and tranquility,
Tender and weak,
purely simple and unadorned,
not mixed with external things,
thus attaining the Way of Heaven and Earth,
therefore they are called Zhēnrén (真 人, True Persons).
Zhēnrén (真 人, True Persons) are those who
magnify themselves and diminish the world,
value cultivating themselves and despise governing others,
do not let things disrupt their harmony,
do not let desires disorder their emotions,
conceal their names and identities,
hide when the Way prevails,
appear when the Way is absent,
act through non-action (wéi wú wéi, 為 無 為),
engage in affairs through non-affairs (shì wú shì, 事 無 事),
know the unknowable,
embrace the Great Way,
encompass the Mind of Heaven,
exhale and inhale Yin and Yang,
expel the old and take in the new,
close with Yin,
open with Yang,
contract and expand with strength and gentleness,
bow and raise their heads with Yin and Yang,
share the same mind with Heaven,
and embody the Way.
They have nothing to enjoy,
nothing to suffer,
Having nothing to be happy about,
having nothing to be angry about,
the myriad things are mysteriously the same,
with no right and no wrong.
Now, if the body is harmed by the abuse of cold, heat, dryness, and dampness,
the body is diminished, but the spirit is strengthened.
If the spirit is harmed by the affliction of joy, anger, thought, and worry,
the spirit is exhausted, and the body is in excess.
Therefore, the true person uses the mind
to restore their nature and rely on the spirit,
supporting each other to attain the beginning and the end.
Therefore, when they sleep, they do not dream,
and when they wake, they have no worries.
Kǒngzǐ asked about the Dao.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Straighten your form,
unify your vision,
the harmony of Heaven will arrive.
Gather your knowledge,
correct your measures,
the spirit will come to reside.
Virtue will make room for you,
the Dao will be your dwelling.
Be like a newborn calf,
with eyes wide open,
not seeking its cause.
Let your form be like a withered tree,
If the heart is like dead ashes,
truly and in reality, knowing without stubbornly clinging to distorted reasons,
being vast and boundless with no heart to scheme,
"being clear and understanding in all directions,
how can one be ignorant?"
Lǎozǐ said:
Now, the conduct of affairs arises from responding to changes,
changes arise from the times,
those who know the times have no fixed conduct.
Therefore,
"The Dao that can be spoken of
is not the constant Dao;
the name that can be named
is not the constant name."
Writings are what give rise to words,
words come from wisdom,
the wise do not know,
(this) is not the constant Dao;
the name that can be named,
is not the one who treasures books.
"Much learning leads to frequent exhaustion;
it is better to guard the center,"
"Abandon learning, and you will have no worries,"
"Abandon sageliness, discard wisdom,
and the people will benefit a hundredfold."
People are born in stillness,
which is the nature of Heaven;
To be moved by external things is
the desire of one's nature.
To respond when things arrive is
the action of wisdom.
When wisdom comes into contact with things,
likes and dislikes are born.
When likes and dislikes take shape,
wisdom goes outward,
unable to turn back to oneself,
and the heavenly principle is extinguished.
Therefore, the sage does not use human (actions) to replace the heavenly (order).
Outwardly, he transforms with things, but inwardly he does not lose his true feelings.
Therefore, one who is enlightened in the Dao
returns to purity and stillness;
one who investigates things
ultimately arrives at non-action.
He nourishes wisdom with tranquility,
and unites spirit with indifference.
He approaches that which has no gate.
One who follows Heaven wanders with the Dao;
one who follows man consorts with the vulgar.
Therefore, the sage does not let affairs erode the heavenly,
nor let desires disorder his feelings.
He hits the mark without scheming,
is trusted without speaking,
attains without deliberating,
and accomplishes without acting.
Therefore, when he occupies a high position, the people do not feel burdened;
To be ahead without harming others,
the world will turn to him,
the treacherous and evil will fear him,
because he does not contend with the myriad things,
therefore none dare contend with him.
Lǎozǐ said:
Indeed, people who follow their desires lose their nature,
and their actions are never correct.
To govern a country with this leads to chaos,
to cultivate oneself with this leads to impurity.
Therefore, one who does not hear the Dao,
has no way to return to his true nature.
One who does not understand things,
cannot achieve purity and tranquility.
Originally, human nature is without crookedness or impurity,
but prolonged immersion in things easily alters it.
Altered and forgetting its origin, it then conforms to a likeness of nature.
The nature of water is to be clear,
but sand and stones pollute it;
the nature of man is to be balanced,
but desires harm it.
Only the sage can abandon external things and return to himself.
Therefore, the sage does not use wisdom to enslave things,
nor does he allow desires to disrupt harmony.
In joy, he is not excessively delighted,
in sorrow, he is not excessively grieved,
therefore he is high but not in danger,
To be secure and not to topple.
Therefore, upon hearing good words and expedient plans,
even a fool knows to speak of them.
Upon praising sagely virtues and lofty conduct,
even the unworthy know to admire them.
There are many who speak of them, but few who employ them;
there are many who admire them, but few who practice them.
The reason for this is
being drawn to material things and bound by customs.
Therefore it is said:
"I take no action, yet the people transform themselves;
I am without affairs, yet the people enrich themselves;
I love stillness, yet the people correct themselves;
I have no desires, yet the people return to simplicity."
Purity and tranquility are the pinnacle of virtue;
gentleness and weakness are the application of the Dao;
emptiness, nothingness, tranquility and pleasure are the origin of all things.
These three, when practiced, dissolve into the formless.
The formless
is what is meant by "the One."
The One
is without intention, yet conforms to all under Heaven.
Spreading virtue without exhaustion,
employing it without diligence,
looking at it, it cannot be seen,
listening to it, it cannot be heard.
From the formless, form is born;
from the soundless, the five tones resound;
Flavorless, and yet the five flavors are formed;
colorless, and yet the five colors are brought into being.
Therefore, existence arises from non-existence,
and substance arises from emptiness.
The number of musical tones does not exceed five,
but the variations of the five tones cannot be fully listened to.
The number of flavors does not exceed five,
but the variations of the five flavors cannot be fully tasted.
The number of colors does not exceed five,
but the variations of the five colors cannot be fully observed.
With the establishment of the *gōng* note, the five tones are formed;
with the establishment of sweetness, the five flavors are determined;
with the establishment of whiteness, the five colors are formed;
with the establishment of the One, the myriad things come into being.
Therefore, the principle of the One
extends to the four seas;
the blessing of the One
is discerned in heaven and earth.
In its entirety,
it is substantial, seemingly like uncarved wood;
in its dispersion,
it is vast, seemingly like muddy water.
Muddy, and yet it slowly clears;
empty, and yet it slowly fills;
placid, like a great sea;
boundless, like floating clouds;
seemingly non-existent, yet it exists;
seemingly lost, yet it remains.
Lǎozǐ yuē:
"The totality of all things,
all pass through a single aperture;
the root of all affairs,
all issue from a single gate.
Therefore, the sage adheres to a single standard and follows a fixed course,
not altering what is past,
not changing what is constant.
He sets the standard and follows the line;
deviations are corrected by that which is constant.
Now, joy and anger
are deviations from the Dao;
worry and sorrow
are losses of virtue;
likes and dislikes
are excesses of the mind;
cravings and desires
are burdens on life.
Great anger injures the *yin*;
great joy weakens the *yang*;
suppressed anger leads to speechlessness;
fright and terror cause madness;
worry and sorrow burn the heart;
illnesses then accumulate.
If a person can eliminate these five,
then they will be in accord with spiritual illumination.
Spiritual illumination
To obtain it internally,
those who obtain it internally,
the five viscera are at peace,
thoughts and worries are calm,
the ears and eyes are acute and clear,
the sinews and bones are strong and firm,
flowing freely and not obstructed,
strong and unyielding and never exhausted,
with nothing in excess,
and nothing lacking.
In all the world, nothing is more soft and weak than water,
this is the way of water.
Its breadth is immeasurable,
its depth unfathomable,
its length reaches infinity,
its distance is endlessly profound.
Its waxing, waning, decreasing, and increasing,
exceeds all calculation.
Ascending, it becomes rain and dew for the heavens,
descending, it becomes moisture and luster for the earth.
All things must be born by it,
all affairs must be accomplished by it.
It generously encompasses all living beings without personal preference,
its beneficence reaches even the smallest insects (qí'áo) without seeking reward.
It enriches and sustains the world without being depleted,
it bestows virtue upon the people without cost.
Its course cannot be completely traced,
its subtlety cannot be grasped.
You may strike it, but it is not bruised;
you may pierce it, but it is not wounded;
you may chop at it, but it is not severed;
you may scorch it, but it is not singed.
It is supple and flowing, circulating and impossible to grind down and scatter.
It can penetrate metal and stone,
strongly aid the world,
sometimes abundant, sometimes scarce,
letting the world take and give freely.
It receives all things without preference,
without selfishness or bias,
and is vast and identical with Heaven and Earth.
This is called supreme virtue.
The reason why water is able to achieve its supreme virtue
is because of its suppleness, smoothness, and lubrication.
Therefore it is said:
"The softest thing in the world
gallops across the hardest thing in the world;
nothing can enter where there is no space."
That which is without form
is the great ancestor of things;
that which is without sound
is the great ancestor of all beings.
The true person (zhēn rén)
is one whose spirit is thoroughly connected to the spiritual abode,
who acts as a person in harmony with the Creator,
who holds profound virtue in their heart,
and whose transformations are as swift as a god.
Therefore, the Dao of the Dao that cannot be spoken of,
is vast indeed!
It is that which transforms customs and changes habits without issuing commands or decrees;
it is solely that which operates through the mind.
The myriad things have a source of life, and each alone knows to guard its root;
the hundred affairs have a point of origin, and each alone knows to guard its gate.
Therefore, one can exhaust the inexhaustible,
reach the unreachable,
illuminate things without being dazzled,
respond to sounds without knowing how.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Now, those who attain the Dao,
their will is weak, but their actions are strong;
their heart is empty, but their responses are appropriate."
A weak will is gentle, soft, and peaceful,
hidden in not daring,
acting in the guise of inability,
calm and non-assertive,
moving without losing the opportune moment,
hence,
"Nobility must take lowliness as its foundation,
height must take what is below as its base."
Entrusting to the small to encompass the large,
being in the center to control the outside,
acting with gentleness, yet being strong,
there is no force that cannot be overcome,
no enemy that cannot be subdued,
Responding to transformations and measuring the times,
nothing can harm it.
If you desire strength, you must preserve it with gentleness.
If you desire power, you must protect it with weakness.
Accumulating gentleness becomes strength;
accumulating weakness becomes power.
Observe what is accumulated
to know existence and destruction.
Force that conquers those inferior to itself
will be resisted when it encounters its equal.
Gentleness that conquers those superior to itself
has a power that cannot be measured.
Therefore,
"A strong army is destroyed,
a strong tree is broken."
Stiff leather is cracked,
teeth are harder than the tongue but wear out first.
Therefore,
"Gentleness and weakness are the trunk of life;
firmness and strength are the followers of death."
Taking the lead is the path to exhaustion;
moving later is the source of attainment.
To grasp the Dao and respond to change,
the one who acts first can also control the one who acts later,
and the one who acts later can also control the one who acts first.
Why is this?
If you do not lose that with which you control others,
others also cannot control you.
What is meant by "the latter"
is to adjust its numbers and accord with the times.
The reversals of the times
allow no interval for rest.
To precede it is to greatly exceed,
to follow it is to fall short.
The sun revolves and the moon circles;
time does not wait for people.
Therefore, the sage does not value a foot-long *bì* jade disc
but values an inch of time,
as time is hard to get and easily lost.
Therefore, the sage acts in accordance with the times,
and establishes merit based on resources.
He guards the pure *dào*,
adheres to the female principle,
follows the course and responds to change,
is always behind and never ahead,
is gentle and weak, using stillness,
is calm and slow, achieving stability.
His merit is great and unbreakable;
none can contend with him.
Lǎozǐ said:
If a calculating mind is hidden within,
then pure whiteness is not unmixed,
and spiritual virtue is not complete.
If one does not know what is near to oneself,
how can one embrace what is far away?
One who forgets the intention to harm others in their heart,
can even grab the tail of a hungry tiger.
How much more so with people?
One who embodies the Dao is at ease and never exhausted,
while one who relies on calculations labors without success.
Harsh laws and cruel punishments
are not the work of an emperor;
frequent use of whips and spurs
is not the way to drive a carriage far.
Excessive likes and dislikes
will inevitably bring misfortune.
Therefore, the laws of the former kings were not something they created,
but something they inherited;
their prohibitions and punishments were not something they initiated,
but something they maintained.
Thus, that which can be inherited becomes great,
while that which is created becomes small;
that which can be maintained becomes secure,
while that which is initiated ends in failure.
Those who rely on their ears and eyes to listen and see
trouble their minds and gain no clear understanding.
Those who rely on their intelligence and deliberation to govern
afflict their hearts and achieve nothing.
Relying on the talent of a single person is insufficient to achieve good governance.
The ability of one person is not even enough to manage a three-*mǔ* house.
By following the principles of reason,
and relying on the natural order of Heaven and Earth,
That is to say, even the entire universe (liù hé) is not perfectly balanced.
The ears are misled by biased praise and criticism;
the eyes are seduced by bright colors;
mere rituals are certainly insufficient to prevent indulgence;
sincere heart can cherish those who are distant.
Therefore, nothing is more devastating than the mind;
and the Mò yé sword is secondary.
No enemy is greater than the principles of Yin and Yang;
and the drum and drumstick are insignificant.
The so-called great enemy lies in the dead and doesn't speak of restraint;
the medium enemy is hidden in the mountains;
the small enemy is hidden among the people.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the people have much intelligence,
strange things arise in abundance;
when laws and decrees become increasingly clear,
bandits and thieves abound."
Abandon the former and adopt the latter,
and heavenly disaster will not arise.
"Therefore, using intelligence to govern a state
is the state's bane;
not using intelligence to govern a state
is the state's virtue."
Heaven is formless and thus vast,
while that which has form is small.
That which is formless is abundant,
while that which has form is scarce.
That which is formless is strong,
Yǒuxíng (有形) is weak;
Wúxíng (無形) is substantial.
Yǒuxíng (有形) is empty;
that which has form completes tasks;
that which has no form initiates beginnings.
Completing tasks results in finished vessels;
initiating beginnings results in simplicity.
That which has form has sound;
that which has no form has no sound.
That which has form is produced from that which has no form;
therefore, that which has no form is the origin of that which has form.
Extensiveness and thickness have names;
that which has a name values completeness.
Thrift and thinness have no name;
that which has no name is deemed cheap and light.
Abundance and wealth have names;
that which has a name is esteemed and favored.
Poverty and scarcity have no name;
that which has no name is considered lowly and disgraced.
Male and stallion have names;
that which has a name manifests virtue.
Female and mare have no name;
that which has no name is hidden and obscure.
That which is surplus has a name;
that which has a name is noble and virtuous.
That which is insufficient has no name;
that which has no name is assigned to lower tasks.
Having merit results in having a name;
Without merit, there is no fame.
Fame is produced from obscurity.
Obscurity is the mother of fame.
Now, the Dao,
"[Existence and non-existence produce each other,
difficulty and ease complete each other]."
Therefore, the sage holds to the Dao, embracing emptiness and tranquility,
subtlety and profundity, to perfect his virtue.
Thus, having the Dao means having virtue;
having virtue means having merit;
having merit means having fame;
having fame means returning to the Dao.
Merit and fame last long,
and throughout life, there is no blame.
Kings and dukes have merit and fame,
the orphaned and widowed have no merit or fame.
Therefore, it is said:
"The sage calls himself orphaned and widowed."
Returning to its root,
accomplishing merit without possessing it.
Therefore, having merit is considered beneficial,
and having obscurity is considered useful.
In ancient times, the people were naive and ignorant,
not knowing east from west.
Their appearance did not deviate from their true feelings,
their words did not depart from their actions,
their actions arose without pretense,
their words were not embellished.
Their clothing is warm but without color,
their weapons are blunt and without edge,
they walk with stumbling steps,
they see with dim eyes,
they dig wells and drink,
they till fields and eat,
they do not give alms,
they do not seek virtue,
high and low do not encroach on each other,
long and short do not compare themselves,
following the customs of the age is easy,
things being completely within one’s ability is easy to do,
to be pretentious and false in order to delude the world,
and to act strangely in order to confuse the masses,
the sage does not consider that to be popular custom.
Essence and sincerity.
Lǎozǐ said:
Heaven achieves its height,
earth achieves its thickness,
the sun and moon shine,
the stars are bright,
the *yīn* and *yáng* are harmonious;
it is not done through deliberate effort,
but by rectifying its course and things naturally follow.
The *yīn* and *yáng* and the four seasons do not produce the myriad things,
the rain and dew falling in due season do not nourish the grasses and trees;
when the spiritual and the bright connect,
When *yīn* and *yáng* are in harmony,
the myriad things come into being.
Now, the Dao
stores essence within,
lodges spirit in the heart,
is quiet, still, tranquil, and serene,
delights and harmonizes the breast,
is vast and formless,
is silent and soundless.
If the government offices are as if without affairs,
the court as if without people,
there are no hermits,
no recluses,
no burdensome labors,
no wrongful punishments,
then all under Heaven will not but admire the ruler's virtue,
and emulate the sovereign's purpose.
Even faraway countries and different customs will not but arrive through multiple interpreters,
not necessarily by personally visiting each household and seeing each individual,
but by extending their sincere heart
and applying it to all under Heaven.
Therefore, rewarding good and punishing violence
are matters of government and command;
the reason they can be carried out
is because of utmost sincerity.
Commands, though clear, cannot be carried out alone;
they must await utmost sincerity.
Therefore, if you comprehensively guide the Dao to cover the people, but the people do not follow,
(If) utmost sincerity does not arrive (i.e., reach its destination).
Lǎozǐ said:
Heaven establishes the sun and moon,
Arranges the stars and constellations,
Spreads out the four seasons,
Regulates yin and yang;
The sun exposes them (to its heat),
The night allows them to rest,
The wind dries them,
Rain and dew moisten them;
In its nourishing of living things,
None see where it nurtures them, yet all things grow;
In its killing of living things,
None see where it destroys them, yet all things perish.
This is called divine intelligence.
Therefore, the sage emulates it,
In his arousing of blessings,
(People) do not see the reason why, yet blessings arise;
In his removing of disasters,
(People) do not see the cause whereby, yet disasters are removed.
To investigate it is impossible to grasp,
To examine it is not in vain,
Daily calculation is insufficient,
Yearly reckoning is more than enough,
(It is) silent and without sound,
(Yet) one word greatly moves the world;
This is how the heart of Heaven influences and transforms.
Therefore, when utmost sincerity takes internal form,
the vital energy moves Heaven.
Auspicious stars appear,
yellow dragons descend,
phoenixes arrive,
sweet springs flow,
excellent grains grow,
the Yellow River does not overflow,
and the seas do not surge with waves.
Act against Heaven and treat things violently,
and then the sun and moon will be eclipsed,
the five planets will lose their course,
the four seasons will become disordered,
daytime will be dark, and nighttime will be bright,
mountains will collapse and rivers will dry up,
winter will have thunder, and summer will have frost.
Heaven and humanity,
have means of communication with each other.
Therefore, when a state is about to perish,
astronomical signs change,
customs become chaotic,
rainbows and secondary rainbows appear.
All things are connected,
essential energies mutually affect each other.
Therefore, matters of the spirits and the divine
cannot be accomplished by wisdom and skill,
nor can they be brought about by force.
Therefore, the great person (dà rén) unites their virtue with Heaven and Earth,
To be united in brightness with the sun and moon,
to be united in spirituality with the spirits,
to be united in trustworthiness with the four seasons,
to cherish the heart of Heaven,
to embrace the qi of Earth,
to hold fast to the void, encompassing harmony,
without leaving the hall, to travel the four seas,
transforming customs and habits,
the people are reformed and move towards goodness,
as if it all originates from oneself;
such is one who can transform through spirit.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Now, the way of humans
is to fully realize one's nature and preserve one's true self,
without harming one's body.
Encountering urgent difficulties,
one's essence communicates with Heaven.
If one has never departed from one's origin,
what would one do that would not succeed?
Life and death share the same realm,
and cannot be threatened or violated.
Moreover, one who governs Heaven and Earth,
oversees all things,
befriends creation,
and encompasses utmost harmony,
has never truly died.
Sincere essence takes shape within,
and outwardly enlighten the human heart.
This is the Way that cannot be transmitted through words.
When the sage is in a position of leadership,
he cherishes the Way but does not speak of it.
His beneficence reaches the myriad people,
therefore, the teaching that comes from silence
is exceedingly great!
When ruler and minister are at odds,
their deceitfulness is revealed to Heaven.
Spirit and breath respond to each other,
making the signs manifest.
This is called the argument that needs no words,
the Way that cannot be spoken.
To summon those afar, let them feel non-interference.
To keep those nearby, speak as if there is nothing of consequence.
Only those who walk at night can truly understand this.
Hence, if one turns back a running horse to fertilize the fields,
then cart tracks will not reach beyond distant lands.
This is called sitting still while galloping, silently sinking.
The Way of Heaven is impartial; it neither approaches
nor departs out of self-interest.
The capable have more than enough,
while the clumsy lack what they need.
Those who follow it benefit,
those who go against it meet with misfortune.
Therefore, those who govern by intellect find it difficult to maintain their state.
Only those who harmonize with the Great Harmony and uphold the natural response
are truly capable.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Now, the relationship between the Dao and Virtue,
is like cured leather and raw hide.
If you distance yourself from it, it becomes near;
if you draw near to it, it becomes distant.
Examine it, and you cannot grasp it;
observe it, and you find it is not empty."
Therefore, the sage is like a mirror,
neither sending off nor welcoming,
responding without storing,
transforming with all things without being harmed.
Gaining it [the Dao],
is in fact losing it;
losing it,
is in fact gaining it.
Therefore, one who understands the Great Harmony
is dimly like someone deeply drunk, peacefully sleeping and wandering within it,
as if never having left its origin.
This is called Great Understanding.
This is to borrow what is not able to accomplish its function."
Lǎozǐ said:
"In the past, when Huángdì governed the world,
he regulated the movements of the sun and moon,
controlled the Qi of Yin and Yang,
regulated the measures of the four seasons,
rectified the calculations of the musical scales and calendar,
Distinguish between men and women;
Clarify the hierarchy between superiors and inferiors;
Ensure the strong do not oppress the weak;
Ensure the many do not tyrannize the few;
The people can preserve their lives and not die prematurely;
The years are ripe with harvest and not plagued by famine;
All officials are upright and selfless;
Superiors and inferiors are in harmony without resentment;
Laws and regulations are clear and not obscure;
Assistants are impartial and not biased;
Farmers yield the boundary of their fields;
People do not pick up lost items on the road;
Merchants do not predetermine prices in the market;
Therefore, during this time,
The sun, moon, and stars do not deviate from their courses;
Wind and rain come at the proper seasons;
The five grains flourish abundantly;
The phoenixes fly in the courtyard;
The qílín (麒麟) roam in the suburbs.
When Fúxī Shì (虙犧氏) ruled the world,
He used a stone for a pillow and a rope for a bed;
He executed criminals in the autumn and made agreements in the winter;
He carried the square continent,
Embraced the round sky,
He unblocked the obstructed and stagnant places where *yīn* and *yáng* were trapped;
He stopped those things accumulating deeply, such as perverse *qì* and violent actions that injured the people;
He stopped them.
His people were innocent and did not know east from west;
Eyesight is dim,
walking is unsteady,
yet he is serenely content with himself,
not knowing the source of it all.
He floats around aimlessly,
not knowing his origins.
He nourishes himself without knowing where he's going.
At this time,
birds, beasts, insects, and snakes all conceal their claws and teeth,
hide their stingers and venom,
and measure the achievements of Heaven and Earth.
Even the Zhòng Huángdì approached the remote and mysterious Tàizǔ,
yet he did not proclaim his achievements,
did not publicize his name,
but concealed the Way of the True Person,
to accord with the natural constancy of Heaven and Earth.
Why?
Because when virtue and the Way are in complete accord,
cleverness and contrivance disappear.
Lǎozǐ said:
If Heaven were not constant,
the sun and moon would have nothing to rest upon;
if Earth were not constant,
plants and trees would have nothing to stand upon;
if the self were not tranquil,
right and wrong would have no form.
Therefore, only with the True Person can there be true knowledge.
If what one holds to is unclear,
how can one know that what I call knowing is not knowing?
Accumulating kindness and heavy wealth,
causing the people to be delighted,
and causing people to enjoy their lives,
this is rén (仁, benevolence);
undertaking great achievements,
displaying a distinguished reputation,
regulating the relationship between ruler and subject,
correcting the relationship between superiors and inferiors,
clarifying the relationship between close relatives and distant relatives,
preserving endangered states,
continuing extinguished lineages,
and establishing heirs for those who have none,
this is yì (義, righteousness);
closing the nine orifices,
concealing intentions and desires,
abandoning cleverness,
returning to ignorance,
drifting vaguely outside the defilement of the world,
wandering freely in a state of non-affairs,
containing yin and exhaling yang, harmonizing with all things,
this is dé (德, virtue).
Therefore, the Dào (道, the Way) scatters and becomes dé,
dé overflows and becomes rén and yì,
and when rén and yì are established, dé and Dào are abandoned.
Lǎo Zǐ (老子) said:
Those whose spirit exceeds (their substance) have flowery words;
those whose virtue is dissipated have hypocritical actions.
When the utmost essence is lost within,
and words and actions are observed from the outside,
this cannot avoid using the body to serve things.
Essence has its limits of depletion, but actions have no end.
What is guarded is not fixed, and the outside is dissolute in the customs of the world.
Therefore, the sage cultivates virtue and morality internally but does not outwardly adorn with benevolence and righteousness.
He understands the suitability of the nine orifices and four limbs,
and wanders in the harmony of spirit.
This is the wandering of the sage.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said:
"As for the wandering of the sage,
he moves in the utmost emptiness,
his mind wanders in the Great Nothing,
he gallops beyond the square,
he walks through the gateless,
he listens to the soundless,
he sees the formless,
he is not constrained by the world,
he is not bound by customs."
Therefore, what the sage uses to move the world,
the True Man does not exceed;
what the wise man uses to correct the world's customs,
the sage does not observe.
The person constrained by worldly customs
inevitably has their form bound and their spirit leaking out,
Therefore, not being free from troubles,
and allowing me to be restrained and bound,
must mean that my fate lies outside of myself.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said:
"The thoughts of the ruler
do not let the spirit wander within his breast,
nor does wisdom extend beyond the four borders.
Cherishing a heart of benevolence and sincerity,
sweet rain comes in due season,
and the five grains flourish;
spring brings life and summer brings growth,
autumn brings harvest and winter brings storage;
monthly inspections and seasonal examinations
result in annual tributes being offered.
Nurturing the people with impartiality,
awe-inspiring power is not used,
laws are simple and not cumbersome,
instruction and transformation are like magic,
laws are lenient and punishments are light,
prisons are empty,
the world is unified in custom,
and no one harbors treacherous thoughts.
This is the grace of the sage."
If the ruler is fond of taking without limit,
then those below will covet achievement without yielding.
The people will be poor and suffering, and disputes will arise;
their labor will be toilsome and without benefit,
When cunning and deception arise,
bandits and thieves multiply.
Those above and those below resent each other,
orders and commands are not carried out.
Now, when water is muddy, the fish gasp for air;
when the government is harsh, the people rebel.
When those above have many desires, then those below have much deceit;
when those above are troublesome, then those below are unsettled;
when those above demand much, then those below compete with each other.
To not govern the root and instead try to remedy the branches
is no different than digging a ditch to stop the water,
or carrying firewood to extinguish a fire.
The sage's affairs are simple and easy to govern,
his desires are few and easy to satisfy.
He is benevolent without exerting benevolence,
he is trustworthy without speaking,
he obtains without seeking,
he achieves without doing.
He embraces nature,
preserves utmost sincerity,
cherishes the Dao and promotes sincerity.
The world follows him as an echo responds to sound,
or a shadow imitates form.
What he cultivates is the root.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"If the spirit wanders outside,
and wisdom and thought rove within,
If one cannot govern the physical body,
and the use of one's spirit extends far,
then what is neglected will be near.
Therefore,
"Without going out the door, one can know the world;
without peeking through the window, one can know the Dao of Heaven.
The further one goes out,
the less one knows."
This speaks of the refined essence arising from within,
and the vital energy moving Heaven.
Lǎozǐ said:
The sun in winter,
the shade in summer,
all things return to them without being commanded.
They are the ultimate, natural, and most refined influence.
They come without being summoned,
and go without being bidden.
Deep and obscure,
without knowing what they do, yet their accomplishments are naturally achieved.
To rely on the eyes to see,
to rely on words to give commands,
is difficult to govern with.
Gāoyáo was mute yet served as Grand Justice,
and there were no cruel punishments in the land.
What value, then, is there in speech?
Shī Kuàng was blind yet served as Grand Minister,
and there were no chaotic policies in the state of Jìn.
What is valued in seeing (a ruler) is this:
his commands are unspoken,
his vision is unseen.
This is how the sage becomes a teacher.
The people are transformed by their superiors,
not following what they say, but following what they do.
Therefore, if a ruler is fond of bravery,
even if he does not encourage fighting, the state will have many troubles,
and gradually there will inevitably be rebellions with assassinations.
If a ruler is fond of sensual pleasure,
even if he does not encourage gossip and criticism, the state will be muddled and chaotic,
and its accumulation will lead to the disaster of dissolute excess.
Therefore, the sage's sincerity takes shape within,
and his likes and dislikes are clear externally.
He speaks words that match his feelings,
and issues commands with clear intent.
Therefore, punishments are not enough to change customs,
and executions are not enough to stop wrongdoing.
Only spiritual transformation is valued.
Perfect sincerity reaches the level of the divine.
What perfect sincerity moves
is like the birth of spring energy
or the killing power of autumn energy.
Therefore, the ruler of men
is like an archer:
what is a hair's breadth here
becomes a common measurement there!
Therefore, one who governs people
Be cautious about that by which you influence others.
Lǎozǐ said:
To establish laws and set up rewards yet fail to transform customs and change habits,
is because a sincere heart is not embraced.
Therefore, by listening to their sounds, one knows their customs;
by observing their music, one knows their habits;
by seeing their habits, one knows their transformation.
Those who embrace truth and demonstrate sincerity
move Heaven and Earth;
divine pronouncements are from beyond the region;
commands are carried out, and prohibitions are heeded.
Sincerity penetrates their Dao and conveys their intent.
Even without a single word,
all people under Heaven,
birds and beasts,
and ghosts and spirits will transform with them.
Therefore, the highest (ruler) transforms divinely;
the next best prevents people from doing wrong;
the lowest rewards the worthy and punishes the violent.
Lǎozǐ said:
The Great Dao is non-action (無為, wúwéi);
non-action is non-being;
that which is non-being does not dwell (anywhere);
that which does not dwell is in a formless state;
that which is formless does not move;
that which does not move is without words;
That which is without speech is stillness and silence.
That which is without form and sound,
when looked at, cannot be seen;
when listened to, cannot be heard.
This is called subtle.
This is called supremely divine.
"[Mián mián ruò cún],"
"This is called the root of Heaven and Earth."
The Dao is without form and sound.
Therefore, the sage forces it to have a form,
and uses one word as its name:
the Dao of Heaven and Earth.
The great takes the small as its origin.
The many begin with the few.
The Son of Heaven models himself on Heaven and Earth,
and takes the myriad things as resources.
His merit and virtue are supremely great.
His power and name are supremely noble.
The beauty of his two virtues matches Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, he must not fail to follow the Great Dao and become the mother of the world.
Lǎozǐ said:
Relieving the poor and helping the needy creates a reputation.
Creating benefits and eliminating harm brings about the completion of accomplishments.
If the world is without disasters,
even a sage will have no place to exercise his virtue.
If those above and below are harmonious,
even the wise will have no place to establish his merit.
Therefore, the governance of the most perfect person
contains virtue and embraces the Dao.
They extend sincerity and joyfully bestow benefits.
They embrace infinite wisdom,
remaining silent and not speaking.
The world does not know to value their silence.
Therefore,
"The Dao that can be spoken of
is not the constant Dao;
the name that can be named
is not the constant name."
That which is written on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
and can be transmitted to others,
is all its coarseness.
The Three Sovereigns (Sānhuáng), Five Emperors (Wǔdì), and Three Kings (Sānwáng),
had different affairs but the same heart,
different paths but the same destination.
This is the learning of later ages.
They do not understand where the Dao is unified as one body,
where Virtue's essence lies.
They take the traces of accomplished deeds
and speak of them while kneeling and sitting.
Though they are broadly learned and have heard much,
they cannot avoid chaos.
Lǎozǐ said:
The essence of the mind
It can be deified,
but not explained in words.
The sage does not descend from his mat, yet rectifies the world.
Affection is deeper than calling out.
Therefore, though the words are the same, the people believe them;
belief lies before the words.
Though the commands are the same, they are carried out;
sincerity lies beyond the commands.
When the sage is above,
the people are transformed as if by magic.
Affection comes first.
If movement above does not elicit response below,
it is because affection and commands differ.
A three-month-old infant does not know benefit or harm,
yet its loving mother instructs it with love,
that is affection.
Therefore, the transformation caused by the use of words is small;
how small!
The transformation caused by the use of silence is great;
how great!
Trustworthiness is the word of the *jūnzǐ* (君子, a gentleman);
loyalty is the intention of the *jūnzǐ*;
when loyalty and trustworthiness take shape within,
emotion and response accord without—
this is the transformation wrought by the worthy sages.
*Lǎozǐ* (老子) said:
"A son dying for his father,
My dying is for my lord.
It is not to seek fame through death.
It is the kindness hidden in my heart that does not shrink from difficulty.
The sorrow of a *jūnzǐ* 君子 is not something deliberately put on display,
but arises from within.
Also, examine what one does in the dark.
A sage is not ashamed before the shadow
A *jūnzǐ* 君子 is cautious when alone.
Abandoning what is near for what is far
is a blockage.
Therefore, when a sage is in a high position, the people rejoice in their governance;
when they are in a low position, the people admire their intentions;
their minds never forget the desire to benefit others.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said:
When a brave warrior gives a shout,
the entire army retreats,
because it comes from sincerity.
To lead without being followed,
to have intention without it being carried out,
means there must be something discordant in the heart.
To rectify the world without leaving one's mat
is to seek it within oneself.
Therefore, where words cannot reach,
countenance can.
Where countenance cannot reach,
sudden inspiration can.
Inspiration arises from the heart and takes form.
The utmost refinement of *jīng* (精) can lead to physical connection,
but cannot illuminate the predetermined time.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said:
"Words have a source,
affairs have a root.
If you lose their source and root,
even if your skills are numerous,
they are not as good as having few."
The Dǐng (鼎) of the Zhōu (周) dynasty depicted Chuí (倕) and caused him to have his fingers cut off,
to illustrate that great skill cannot be forced.
Therefore, the intelligence of artisans lies
not in their abilities but in seizing the opportune moment.
Closing, without knowing it is closing;
therefore, one must block before opening.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said:
"When the sage engages in affairs,
the paths they take are different, but they return to the same destination.
Whether in existence or ruin, stability or collapse, they are as one,
their minds never forgetting the desire to benefit others."
Therefore, the songs of Qín (秦), Chǔ (楚), Yān (燕), and Wèi (魏),
have different sounds, yet are all joyful.
The weeping of the Nine Yí (夷) and Eight Dí (狄),
have different sounds, yet are all sorrowful.
Now, singing is a sign of joy,
and weeping is an effect of sorrow.
They resonate within,
It manifests externally;
therefore, it lies in what stimulates it.
The heart of a sage
does not forget, day and night, the desire to benefit others;
the reach of his benevolence is also far.
Lǎozǐ said:
"The people are governed by non-action,
action leads to harm."
Those who govern by non-action
act through non-action,
those who act cannot be without action,
those who cannot be without action
cannot act.
People have spirit without speaking;
speaking leads to harm.
Those who have spirit without speaking
embody nothingness,
harming that which has spirit within its spirit.
Wénzǐ said:
"Fame can be forcibly established,
merit can be forcibly achieved."
Formerly, Nánróng Chú was ashamed that the Way of the Sage was lost only in himself,
and he went south to see Lǎozǐ,
receiving instruction in one word.
His spirit became enlightened,
obstructed areas became unobstructed,
To endure hardship for ten days without eating is
like enjoying a great sacrifice.
Therefore, one’s brilliance illuminates the land within the seas,
one’s name is established for later generations,
one’s wisdom encompasses heaven and earth,
one’s discernment distinguishes the finest autumn down,
one’s praises resound in the Chinese language,
and continue without ceasing to this day.
This is what is meant by a name that can be forcefully established.
Therefore, if the farmer does not exert himself,
the granaries will not be full;
if the official is not diligent,
his sincerity will not be refined;
if the generals and ministers do not strive,
their achievements will not be accomplished;
if kings and dukes are negligent,
later generations will have no name for them.
The perfect man hides his path,
like thunder concealed.
He acts when the time is right,
and establishes merit based on available resources.
Advancing and retreating are not difficult for him;
there is nothing he does not understand.
The perfect man’s refined sincerity manifests inwardly
and virtue flows in all directions.
Seeing benefits for the world,
he rejoices and does not forget;
seeing harm for the world,
Apprehensive, as if having lost something.
"He who worries about the worries of the people,
the people will also worry about his worries;
he who delights in the delights of the people,
the people will also delight in his delights.
Therefore, worrying with the world,
and delighting with the world,
yet not becoming king—
such a thing has never happened."
"The method of the sage
begins in the invisible,
and ends in the unattainable,
dwells in a place that does not collapse,
accumulates in a granary that is never exhausted,
is stored in a treasury that never runs dry;
issuing commands like the source of flowing water,
employing the people in offices where there is no contention,
opening doors that guarantee success,
not undertaking what cannot be accomplished,
not seeking what cannot be obtained,
not dwelling where one cannot remain long,
not doing what cannot be repeated."
The great man practices a policy that is easy to explain,
and the people all obey his commands.
If the commands are obeyed, then they are followed,
leading from small to great.
If the commands are disobeyed, then good becomes harm,
and success becomes failure.
Now, what is meant by a great man?
He is strong within and enlightened without.
His inner strength is like Heaven and Earth,
His outer enlightenment is like the sun and moon.
Heaven and Earth cover and sustain everything,
The sun and moon illuminate everything.
A great man demonstrates goodness to others,
Without changing his principles,
Without altering his constancy.
The world obeys his commands,
Like grass bending to the wind.
If government fails in spring,
The planet Jupiter waxes and wanes,
Not adhering to its usual position.
If government fails in summer,
The planet Mars moves in retrograde.
If government fails in autumn,
The planet Venus is not in its proper place,
Its appearance and disappearance are irregular.
If government fails in winter,
The planet Mercury does not appear in its proper location.
If the four seasons lose their proper governance,
The planet Saturn wavers,
The sun and moon are seen to be reproached,
The five planets are disordered,
A comet appears.
If spring governance is not lost, millet and sorghum will thrive.
If summer governance is not lost, rain will fall on time.
If the autumn governance is not flawed, the people will be prosperous;
if the winter governance is not flawed, the nation will be healthy and peaceful.
*Jiǔ Shǒu* (Nine Guardians)
Lǎozǐ said:
Before Heaven and Earth took shape,
there was obscurity and darkness,
blended together as one.
Silent and clear,
the heavy and dense became Earth,
the refined and subtle became Heaven.
Separating, they became the four seasons;
dividing, they became Yin and Yang.
Refined *qì* becomes humans,
coarse *qì* becomes insects.
The hard and the soft complement each other;
thus, all things are born.
The spirit originates from Heaven,
the bones are rooted in Earth.
The spirit enters its gate,
the bones return to their root.
What of me remains?
Therefore, the sage models Heaven and follows Earth,
not bound by customs,
not seduced by people,
taking Heaven as father,
taking Earth as mother,
taking Yin and Yang as the guiding principle,
The four seasons are a standard.
When the heavens are still, they are clear.
When the earth is settled, it is peaceful.
Those who go against the myriad things die,
Those who comply with them live.
Therefore, stillness and tranquility are the abode of the spirit,
Emptiness and nothingness are where the Dao resides.
Now, the spirit is what is received from heaven,
And the bones are what are endowed by the earth.
"The Dao gives birth to one,
One gives birth to two,
Two gives birth to three,
Three gives birth to the myriad things.
The myriad things carry yin and embrace yang,
Blending their qi to achieve harmony."
Lǎozǐ said:
People are born by receiving the transformations of heaven and earth.
In the first month, there is a paste.
In the second month, there are blood vessels.
In the third month, there is an embryo.
In the fourth month, there is a fetus.
In the fifth month, there are tendons.
In the sixth month, there are bones.
In the seventh month, the form is completed.
In the eighth month, there is movement.
In the ninth month, there is restlessness.
In the tenth month, there is birth.
Once the form is complete,
The five viscera are then differentiated:
The liver governs the eyes.
The lungs govern the nose.
The spleen governs the tongue.
The kidneys govern the ears.
The gallbladder governs the mouth.
The exterior is the surface.
The interior is the inside.
The head's roundness models Heaven.
The feet's squareness resembles Earth.
Heaven has four seasons,
Five Elements,
Nine Luminaries, and three hundred sixty days.
Humans have four limbs,
Five viscera,
Nine orifices, and three hundred sixty joints.
Heaven has wind, rain, cold, and heat.
Humans have taking and giving, joy and anger.
The gallbladder is like clouds.
The lungs are like air.
The spleen is like wind.
The kidneys are like rain.
The liver is like thunder.
Humans resemble Heaven and Earth.
And the heart is their master.
The ears and eyes are the sun and moon.
The blood and qi are the wind and rain.
If the sun and moon lose their course,
Diminution and loss of light;
untimely winds and rains;
destruction and breakage causing calamities;
the five planets losing their courses;
states and kingdoms suffer their misfortune.
The Way of Heaven and Earth,
is supremely vast and great,
yet still regulates its brilliance and light,
and cherishes its spiritual intelligence.
How can human ears and eyes endure prolonged exposure without rest?
How can the spirit and mind gallop forth without exhaustion?
Therefore, the sage guards the inner and does not lose the outer.
Now, blood and qi are the flourishing aspects of humans,
the five viscera are the essence of humans.
If blood and qi can be focused within and not overflow outwards,
then the chest and abdomen will be full, and desires will be few.
If desires are few, then the ears and eyes will be clear, and hearing and sight will be acute and discerning.
Acute and discerning hearing and sight are called "brightness."
If the five viscera can belong to the heart and not be separated,
then the spirit and intention will be victorious, and actions will not be deviant.
The spirit and mind will be flourishing, and the qi will not be scattered.
With hearing, there is nothing unheard;
with sight, there is nothing unseen;
with action, there is nothing unaccomplished;
worries and misfortunes will have no way to enter;
and evil influences cannot attack.
Therefore, those who seek much gain little;
those who see much know little.
Now, the orifices are the windows and doors of the spirit.
Blood and breath are the messengers of the five viscera.
Therefore, if the ears and eyes are licentious in sounds and sights,
then the five viscera will be agitated and unsettled,
the blood and breath will surge and never cease,
and the spirit will gallop about and not be guarded.
Even if the arrival of fortune or misfortune is like a hill or mountain,
there will be no way to recognize it.
Therefore, the sage loves [the senses] but does not overindulge.
The sage truly makes the ears, eyes, and spirit profoundly penetrating,
without being seduced or infatuated by anything.
If the will and breath do not lose their purity and tranquility and have few desires,
the five viscera will be at peace.
If the spirit guards internally the form and body without overstepping,
then looking at the past world externally,
and the internal matters of future events,
one can fully see the space between fortune and misfortune.
Therefore,
"The further one goes out,
the less one knows."
This is to say that the spirit must not be allowed to be externally licentious.
Therefore,
"Excessive colors dazzle the eyes,
causing the eyes to be unclear;
excessive sounds enter the ears,
causing the ears to be deaf;
excessive flavors disorder the mouth,
causing sores to grow in the mouth;
"Going forward or retreating agitates the heart,
causing actions to become reckless and unrestrained."
Therefore, desires cause one's *qì* to become excessive,
and likes and dislikes exhaust one's *jīng*.
If these are not quickly removed,
then one's will and *qì* will be depleted daily.
The reason why people cannot live out their natural lifespan
is because they value life too much.
Only those who do not take life as their purpose
can achieve longevity.
Heaven and earth move and communicate with each other,
all things are gathered and become one.
To know one is to know all; there is nothing one does not know.
To not know one is to know nothing; there is nothing one can know.
I am in the world as one thing,
and things are also things.
Between things and things,
how can they be distinguished?
Desiring life is not something to be preoccupied with,
and hating death is unavoidable.
Disdaining it is not something to hate,
and valuing it is not something to rejoice over.
Accord with its inherent nature and find peace in it,
without daring to go to extremes.
Not daring to go to extremes is the ultimate joy.
3.1. Maintaining Emptiness and Oneness
Lǎozi said:
The so-called sage
adapts his position to the times,
and finds joy in his work according to the occasion.
Now, grief and joy are deviations of virtue,
likes and dislikes are burdens on the mind,
and elation and anger are excesses of the Dao.
Therefore, in life he follows the course of Heaven,
and in death he transforms with things.
In stillness, he harmonizes in virtue with the Yin,
and in motion, he rides the waves with the Yang.
Therefore, the mind is the master of the form,
and the spirit is the treasure of the mind.
If the form labors without rest, it will collapse;
if the essence is used without ceasing, it will be exhausted.
Therefore, the sage follows these principles and dares not transgress them.
He responds to the existent with the non-existent,
and surely investigates its principles;
he receives the substantial with the empty,
and surely explores its details.
Calm, pleased, empty, and still,
he fulfills his life;
he has nothing he neglects,
nothing he favors.
Embracing virtue and nourishing harmony,
he complies with Heaven,
borders with the Dao,
and is neighbor to virtue.
He does not initiate fortune,
Not creating disaster first,
and with life and death not changing one's self,
therefore is called "utmost divinity."
Being divine, one can obtain whatever one seeks,
and accomplish whatever one intends.
3.2. Guarding without Doubleness
Lǎozǐ said:
"If one treats the world lightly, one's spirit will be unburdened;
if one considers the myriad things as trivial, then one's mind will not be confused;
if one equates life and death, then one's intention will not be frightened;
if one aligns with change, then one's understanding will not be deluded."
Now, the perfect person leans on an unyielding pillar,
travels a path without barriers,
draws from an inexhaustible treasury,
and learns from a teacher who is not dead.
There is nowhere he goes that is not successful,
and nothing he encounters that he does not understand.
Bending and stretching, bowing and looking up,
embracing fate without confusion and moving with ease.
Disaster, fortune, benefit, and harm
are not enough to trouble his heart.
Now, one who acts for righteousness can be compelled by benevolence,
but cannot be coerced by arms;
can be stopped by righteousness,
but cannot be swayed by benefits.
The superior person dies for righteousness,
and cannot be kept (from death) by wealth and status.
To act righteously, one should not fear death.
How much less should one fear doing nothing!
The one who does nothing has no burden.
The person without burden
takes the world as a shadow pillar.
Above, observe the standards of the ultimate person;
deeply investigate the meaning of morality and virtue;
below, examine the conduct of the world;
then it is enough to feel ashamed.
Now, those who do not take the world as their concern
are like a drum that is set up for learning.
3.3 Keeping to the Evenness, Three
Lǎozǐ said:
"Esteemed power and abundant profit
are what people covet,
but compared to the body, they are cheap.
Therefore, the sage eats enough to fill his emptiness and connect to the qi,
and wears enough to cover his form and ward off the cold.
He finds satisfaction in what suits his nature and declines excess.
He does not greedily acquire,
nor does he accumulate much.
He clears his eyes so he does not see,
he stills his ears so he does not listen,
he closes his mouth so he does not speak,
he entrusts his heart so he does not worry,
he abandons cleverness,
he returns to primal simplicity,
Resting the spirit,
discarding old knowledge,
without likes or dislikes,
this is called great understanding.
To eliminate impurities and remove burdens,
nothing is better than never having departed from its source;
what could not be accomplished?
Those who understand the harmony of nourishing life
cannot be swayed by profit;
those who comprehend the correspondence between inner and outer
cannot be enticed by power.
Outside of the outside,
is the greatest;
inside of the inside,
is the most valuable.
If one can understand the greatest value,
wherever one goes, one will succeed.
3.4. *Zhōng Yì Sì*
Lǎozǐ said:
Those of old who practiced the Dao,
ordered their emotions and nature,
governed their mental techniques,
nourished themselves with harmony,
maintained themselves with appropriateness,
delighted in the Dao and forgot their lowliness,
were secure in virtue and forgot their poverty.
There are desires that the nature does not want.
It is not that there is no desire but one cannot obtain it.
There are things the heart does not delight in.
It is not that there is no delight but one does not do them.
That which does not benefit one's nature is not used to burden virtue.
That which is not convenient to life is not used to disturb harmony. One does not indulge oneself and give rein to one's desires, but instead controls them.
Such a person can be a model for the world.
He measures his stomach and eats,
measures his form and clothes himself,
makes his dwelling accommodate his body,
and acts in accordance with his feelings.
He has more than enough for the world, but does not possess it.
He entrusts myriad things to others, but does not profit from them.
How could he lose his nature and life for the sake of poverty, wealth, nobility, or baseness!
Those who are like this
can be said to be able to embody the Dao.
3.5. Keeping the Five Purities
Lǎozǐ said:
When people receive *qì* from Heaven,
the ears and eyes perceive sound and color,
the nose and mouth perceive fragrance and stench,
the skin perceives cold and warmth.
These feelings are the same for everyone.
Some die because of them,
some live,
some become gentlemen,
some become petty men.
The means by which they govern are different.
Spirit (shén) is the source of wisdom.
When the spirit is clear, then wisdom is bright.
Wisdom is the storehouse of the mind.
When wisdom is impartial, then the mind is balanced.
People do not use flowing, turbid water as a mirror, but clear, still water.
Because it is clear and still.
Therefore, when the spirit is clear and the mind is balanced, one can then discern the true nature of things.
Therefore, those who use it must rely on non-action.
If a mirror is clear, then dust and grime will not sully it.
If the spirit is clear, then desires will not mislead it.
Therefore, when the mind has a destination,
the spirit is immediately and wholeheartedly present.
Returning to emptiness,
then restlessness dissipates and agitation ceases.
This is the wanderings of a sage.
Therefore, those who governed the world in ancient times
had to understand the true nature of inherent nature and destiny before they could do so.
3.6 Keeping to Genuineness VI
Lǎozǐ said:
As for what are called sages,
they simply suit their emotions,
measure their bellies to eat,
measure their bodies to dress,
and moderate themselves.
Thus, there is no way for a greedy and corrupt heart to arise.
Therefore, those who can possess the world
Surely, one will not use the world for their own purposes;
those who can have a reputation
will certainly not seek it through hurried actions.
Truly understanding the nature of life,
benevolence and righteousness will then naturally follow.
As for spirit, there is nothing to conceal;
the heart has no burdens.
Thoroughly penetrating and openly reaching,
being tranquil and without concerns,
power and profit cannot tempt,
sensual pleasures cannot corrupt,
the eloquent cannot persuade,
the wise cannot move,
the brave cannot frighten.
This is the roaming of the true person.
That which generates life does not itself generate;
that which transforms does not itself transform.
Those who do not understand this Dao,
even if their wisdom governs heaven and earth,
their clarity illuminates the sun and moon,
their eloquence unravels complex arguments,
their words are as polished as metal and stone,
it is still of no benefit to governing the world.
Therefore, the sage does not lose what he guards.
3.7. Guarding Stillness Seven
Lǎozǐ said:
Stillness, silence, tranquility, and indifference
Therefore, in nurturing life,
one should be harmonious, joyful, empty, and without desires.
Thus, one establishes oneself in virtue.
When external things do not disturb the internal, then one's nature attains its proper place.
When stillness and non-action bring harmony, then virtue secures its position.
Nurturing life is for governing the world,
embracing virtue is for completing one's years.
Such a person can be said to embody the Dao.
If this is so,
the blood vessels will have no stagnation,
the five organs will have no accumulated *qì*.
Misfortune and fortune cannot distort or deceive him,
praise and slander cannot defile him.
If one does not have the right era,
who can save him?
If one has the talent
but does not meet the right time,
one's body still cannot escape (fate).
How much more so if one is without the Dao?
Now, those whose eyes discern the tip of an autumn hair
cannot hear the sound of thunder.
Those whose ears are attuned to the sound of gold and jade
cannot see the shape of Mount Tài Shān.
Therefore, if one has a small ambition,
then one greatly forgets something.
Now, the arrival of the myriad things
plucks and pulls at our nature,
snatches and takes our essence.
It is like a spring;
even if you wish not to draw from it,
how can that be possible?
Now, a basin of water, if left clear for days,
one can see one's reflection;
if muddied by just one stir,
it cannot even reflect square or round shapes.
The spirit of man is difficult to clear but easy to muddy;
it is like a basin of water.
3.8. Obeying the Law 8
Lǎozǐ said: The highest sage models Heaven;
the next esteems the worthy;
the lowest employs ministers.
Employing ministers is the way to danger and ruin;
esteeming the worthy is the source of foolishness and delusion.
Modeling Heaven is the way to govern Heaven and Earth.
Taking emptiness and stillness as the primary principle,
emptiness is that which receives everything,
stillness is that which maintains everything.
Knowing the Way of emptiness and stillness,
one can then achieve beginning and end.
Therefore, the sage governs through stillness
and considers movement as chaos.
Thus, it is said: do not disturb, do not provoke,
and all things will naturally clear themselves;
do not frighten, do not shock,
and all things will naturally govern themselves.
This is what is called the Way of Heaven.
3.9. Remaining Weak
Lǎo Zǐ said:
Emperors and dukes regard the world and the state as their homes,
and treat all things as livestock.
Cherishing the greatness of the world,
possessing the abundance of all things,
their vital energy becomes robust, and their ambition grows arrogant.
The great use arms to invade the small,
the small act haughtily and oppress those above.
Their hearts are extravagant and expansive,
like a whirlwind or a torrential rain,
they cannot last long.
Therefore, the sage uses the Way to stabilize them,
holding to unity and non-action,
without diminishing the vital energy,
seeing the small and preserving gentleness,
retreating and not possessing,
taking the rivers and seas as their model.
The rivers and seas do not act,
therefore achievements and fame naturally transform.
Not forceful,
therefore able to complete their reign,
becoming the female of the world,
therefore able to achieve deathlessness.
Self-loving,
therefore able to complete their nobility.
The power of a ruler of ten thousand chariots
uses all things to achieve merit and fame.
Authority and responsibility are extremely important,
and one must not take oneself lightly.
If one takes oneself lightly, merit and fame will not be achieved.
Now, the Dao
achieves greatness through smallness,
and abundance is achieved by prioritizing scarcity.
Therefore, the sage governs the world with the Dao.
Gentleness, weakness, subtlety show the small.
Frugality, miserliness, deficiency shows the scarce.
Seeing the small, one can thus achieve the great.
Seeing the scarce, one can thus achieve the beautiful.
The way of Heaven
suppresses the high and elevates the low,
diminishes the excessive,
and supplements the insufficient.
Rivers and seas dwell in the lowest places,
therefore all under Heaven submit to them and offer tribute.
Therefore, the sage is humble,
showing the lower by being pure, tranquil and yielding,
and showing the insufficient by having an empty mind and nothing.
Seeing the lower, one can thus attain the higher.
Seeing the insufficient, one can thus achieve sageliness.
The self-satisfied do not stand.
The extravagant do not last long.
The strong and unyielding die.
The full and overflowing perish.
A whirlwind and torrential rain do not last all day;
A small valley cannot be filled in a moment.
A whirlwind and sudden rain embody the energy of the violent and strong,
Therefore, they cannot endure and fade away quickly.
A small valley is situated in a place of the violent and strong,
Therefore, it cannot avoid being taken from.
Therefore, the sage holds onto the female principle (cí pìn),
And abandons arrogance and extravagance.
Not daring to embody the energy of the violent and strong,
By holding onto the female principle (cí pìn),
One is able to establish one's maleness (xióng mǔ).
Not daring to be arrogant and extravagant,
One is able to endure for a long time.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
The way of Heaven reverses at its extreme,
Declines when full,
The sun and moon are examples of this.
Therefore, the sage diminishes daily and keeps his vital energy empty, not daring to be self-satisfied.
Advancing daily by way of the female principle (pìn),
His merit and virtue do not decline.
This is the way of Heaven.
The disposition of people is to love the high and hate the low,
Love to gain and hate to lose,
Love profit and hate sickness,
Love honor and hate humiliation,
Love nobility and hate being lowly.
The masses act according to these desires,
Therefore, they cannot succeed;
they grasp,
therefore, they cannot obtain.
Therefore, the sage emulates Heaven,
accomplishing without acting,
obtaining without grasping,
sharing the same feelings with others but following a different path,
therefore, he can endure for a long time.
Therefore, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors had a vessel of admonition,
called the *yòu zhī* (侑卮),
upright when in the middle,
overturning when full.
For when things flourish, they decline;
when the sun is at its zenith, it moves;
when the moon is full, it wanes;
joy ends in sorrow.
Therefore, intelligence and vast wisdom are guarded with foolishness;
extensive learning and broad eloquence are guarded with frugality;
martial strength and bravery are guarded with awe;
wealth and greatness are guarded with narrowness;
bestowing virtue upon the world is guarded with yielding.
These five are how the former kings guarded the world.
"Those who follow this way do not desire fullness,
therefore, they can discard the old and not create the new."
Lǎozǐ said:
The sage closes himself with the *yīn*,
opens himself with the *yáng*,
and can arrive at having no joy;
If there is nothing that is not a source of joy,
then being without anything that is not a source of joy is the ultimate happiness.
Therefore, joy comes from within and extends outward,
and does not come from external sources and extend inward.
Thus, one possesses self-derived joy,
which leads to ultimate attainment,
making one more valuable than the entire world.
The reason for this is
that one uses the world for the sake of the world.
The key to governing the world
lies not in external things but in oneself,
not in others but in one's own person.
If one cultivates oneself properly, all things will be complete.
Therefore, one who understands the theory of the mind
will be free from desires, preferences, likes, and dislikes.
Therefore, there is nothing to be delighted about,
nothing to be angry about,
nothing to enjoy,
nothing to suffer from.
All things are profoundly the same,
without "is" or "is not," without right or wrong.
Therefore, a gentleman (shì) has a fixed doctrine,
a woman has an unchanging way of conduct,
they do not depend on power to be respected,
they do not need wealth to be rich,
they do not need strength to be strong,
they do not profit from goods and wealth,
they do not covet worldly fame,
Do not consider nobility as security,
do not consider lowliness as danger;
let form, spirit, breath, and will each reside in their proper place.
For the form is the dwelling place of life,
the breath is the source of life,
the spirit is the master of life.
If one loses its place, the other two are harmed.
Therefore, if one takes spirit as the master, the form will benefit accordingly;
if one takes form as the master, the spirit will be harmed accordingly.
Those who are greedy and have many desires,
are confused by power and profit,
and allured by fame and position.
Even with knowledge surpassing others,
and a position high in the world,
their spirit gradually diminishes and fades away.
Prolonged indulgence without return,
the form closes off and resists internally,
then there is no way for it to enter.
This is why there are often afflictions of blindness, forgetfulness, and loss of self.
Now, spirit, essence, will, and breath,
are filled and strengthened daily when still,
but are exhausted and aged daily when agitated.
Therefore, the sage maintains and nourishes his spirit,
harmonizes and weakens his breath,
levels and eases his form,
and floats and sinks with the Dao.
In this way, there is nothing among the transformations of the myriad things that he does not encounter,
and there is nothing among the changes in all affairs that he does not respond to.
3.10. Holding to Simplicity
Lǎozǐ said:
The so-called "true person"
is one whose nature aligns with the Dao.
Therefore, possessing as if not possessing,
being full as if empty,
cultivating the inner without governing the outer,
understanding the Great Simplicity,
acting without acting and returning to simplicity.
Embodying the origin and embracing the spirit,
wandering at the root of Heaven and Earth,
dimly rambling beyond the dust and grime,
roaming freely in the business of non-affairs.
Machinery and cleverness
are not carried in the heart,
understanding without artifice,
not changing with things,
seeing the transformations of things,
and guarding their origin.
The mind and will are focused inward,
understanding misfortune and fortune as one,
dwelling without knowing what to do,
acting without knowing where to go.
Knowing without learning,
seeing without looking,
completing without acting,
distinguishing without governing,
Responding when stimulated,
Acting when pressed,
Going when there's no other choice,
Like the brilliance of light,
Like the effect of a shadow,
Taking the Dao as its guide,
Depending on something to be so,
Vast and empty,
Pure, tranquil, and without thoughts,
